utterances.text: Can you distinguish among these soldiers who are considered to be Seselj's men and who declared themselves to be Chetniks and, on the other hand, volunteers of the Serb Radical Party who were sent to the frontlines from Serbia in some areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Is my question sufficiently clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your question is clear, but I didn't know about these radical people, whether they were Chetniks or soldiers from Serbia. I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'll give you some information that the OTP knows about. The OTP has document 0324-97340. I hope that they will be able to find this, as they find it easy to manage e-court. And this document shows that a large group of volunteers of the Serb Radical Party participated in these first battles for Grbavica, because you know that there was fighting for Grbavica 2 and Hrasno as early as April of 1992; have you heard about this fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have that information, nor did I read about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You live in Grbavica 1; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know that I used to live in Grbavica 2 for more than ten years; are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, maybe I was not so well known at the time. In April 1992 - the OTP has this information and they can show you that, Judges - they have a recording of my telephone conversation in which I asked for assistance for a group of volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party who are encircled in Hrasno. I asked for Karadzic or Krajisnik, and I left a message, "If that group which is surrounded does not get help, I will withdraw all the volunteers from all the frontlines." The OTP has this document, and I assume they will show it to you now. If did they don't, we will not discuss it. You are aware that the JNA withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina in May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we have the document here on the screen. It's on the screen. Thank you, Madam Registrar, for having done such a --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But as the witness doesn't know about this fighting in Hrasno in April, maybe we can use this for your information only. This was conducted in April 1992, and this is a transcript of an intercepted conversation, intercepted by the Muslim authorities. It's my conversation with Branislav Gavrilovic and later on with some other people in Pale. The OTP has all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know that the JNA withdrew from Grbavica and all of Bosnia-Herzegovina in May 1992. It had to withdraw by the 19th of May, based on an ultimatum from the West. As an intellectual, you should be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A large number of soldiers simply changed uniforms. They were JNA soldiers and then they became soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, but that's because they had been born in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They came from Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may say so, there were many among them from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Those who were from Serbia, they were volunteers, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that JNA officers, professional officers, who were not from Bosnia-Herzegovina, all had to withdraw by the 19th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But you have to admit that a large number of these officers came back to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you give me an example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came across them, but I didn't know their names. I didn't need to know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Did you ever see Slavko Aleksic's men, whom you refer to as Seselj's men and who identify themselves as Chetniks, looting, stealing things from people's homes in Grbavica? Did you see that with your own eyes, and can you be absolutely sure they were Slavko Aleksic's men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to admit I did not have an opportunity to work for Seselj's men or Chetniks, nor was I able to see them looting anything, because I didn't work in that area. I worked near the playing field and in Ozrenska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said more than once here that this unit of Slavko Aleksic's, which was Seselj's unit or Chetnik unit was part of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We considered them to be one and the same army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Do you have any information to the effect that I issued orders to Slavko Aleksic from Belgrade or that Slavko Aleksic submitted reports about his activities directly to me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what people said, that he received orders from you, but I don't have that information, nor could I have access to such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you identify the soldiers who said this or were they purely rumours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was things people spoke about in the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Tell me, did you ever see people belonging to Slavko Aleksic's unit, Seselj's men or Chetniks, in other words, killing a civilian in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have an opportunity to see that. It wasn't possible for me to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Were you ever able to see these very men, Slavko Aleksic's men, beating a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't able to see that because I wasn't that close to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You're a very useful witness. I expect you to tell the truth, and that's what you're doing. For the sake of Their Honours, please let's have the following document: It's a request based on 92 bis instead of viva voce testimony, and this document is confidential, so we won't read it or show it in public. We know what it refers to. It's a request, and we are interested in pages 32 and 33. This should not be made public. It's for Their Honours to follow, what kind of summary the OTP made of this witness's testimony from 2004. That's pages 32 and 33. So only to be used in the courtroom, internally, and I'm going to quote what there is in the document and I'm not going to violate the principle of confidentiality in any way by doing so. Can we have that, pages 32 and 33. That's not the same document. The document's date is the 24th of January. It is Annex B. If you can't find it, then let's not waste time. I can quote what it says in the summary, and then I'll hand my copy over to the Trial Chamber so that they can see for themselves. Do you agree, Judges, that we make short issue of this? In that document, on page 32, under the name of this witness and with his pseudonym, it says the following: that he will be testifying about the looting of flats by Seselj's volunteers, about daily beatings, killings, and that Slavko Aleksic directly reported to Seselj. This is in Serbian, of course, but hand that over to the Trial Chamber and I'm sure you'll be able to find it in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: What document is this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the Prosecution document dated the 24th of January, 2006. You submitted the document. It is an annex to your document of the 24th of January, a supplement to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... on the screen, it is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now you have it, but the pages don't seem to coincide in English, but I can't follow because I don't know English. Judges, you can find the portion that I read out. Perhaps this is another document from a different period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the text in B/C/S, and this is the translation of English. But the best, I think, is for you, Mr. Seselj, to read out this summary, and then everything will be much simpler that way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just told you, you have it in English on the first page. It says that: [In English] "The looting of apartments by Seselj's volunteers." [Interpretation] There you have it on page 1, that Seselj's volunteers looted apartments, if I got that right, because I don't know English. And then you have the killing and the beatings, where it says that this witness was beaten on a daily basis. And then on the following page, it says that Slavko Aleksic directly reported to me about his activities. You have that in English there as well, and I've interpreted the gist of it, but you can read the whole text. As far as I'm concerned, this is a very important point, because I wish to draw your attention to how the Prosecutor is interpreting witness -- Prosecution witness statements, and had this been accepted under 92 bis, that would have been introduced into evidence and that would have appeared to be the truth. You would have thought that the witness really said that, whereas the witness is very precise and can distinguish between what he saw, what he heard from others about what happened, and so on. He is able to make the distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, what do you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes, it is an objection using the 65 ter summary during the cross-examination of the witness. I believe it is not a very appropriate way to conduct a cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, during cross-examination you're supposed to ask a question. You can use this document as a basis, as a foundation, but you must recall what was said in the document and then ask the witness about his opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I asked the question first. The witness answered. And then I drew your attention, as the Trial Chamber, to this document. The witness said that he'd never -- he never saw Seselj's men looting apartments. He said he never saw them killing civilians. He said he never saw them beating civilians. He never said that they beat civilians. So we're talking about these people whom he identifies as Seselj's men. And he also said that he does not know that something was rumoured and talked about, but he does not know that Slavko Aleksic directed -- directly reported to me about his activities. And from that summary, you see a completely different interpretation by the Prosecutor, and this is more important for me than the entire cross-examination, because I'm showing you once again how unacceptable it is that statements prepared by the Prosecution you accept as being the truth under 92 bis and 92 quater. This is a catastrophe against the interests of justice, if you accept statements prepared by the OTP in that way. And I'd like to continue now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, this is the problem. I had noticed it in the summary in English. You say "Seselj's volunteers." In the written statement, however, the witness never mentioned Seselj's volunteers, he mentioned Seselj's men. But when saying "volunteers," you're giving a special connection to all this notably when you add later on that Aleksic reported to Mr. Seselj. Intellectually, there's a construction, a logical construction behind all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, we quoted exactly what the witness said in the statement, when he said: "Aleksic was his own boss probably reporting to Vojislav Seselj himself." And also regarding the Seselj volunteers or Seselj's men, he says "Seseljevci." It is in B/C/S I think it can be translated -- of course, I don't know B/C/S, but can be translated as "Seselj's men," but I don't see any difference with "Seselj's volunteers." In any case, I don't understand. Mr. Seselj is struggling every day to listen to witnesses as viva voce witnesses, and now we are discussing what, 92 ter witness? We have the witness. We can ask him everything we want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I understood what Mr. Seselj said, it seems that you made a summary regarding Witness 1060. This could have been the summary of a Rule 92 ter procedure or a written statement written under Rule 92 bis. Fine, but this is not the problem. This is the problem: When reading the summary, as it is written, we see that the Prosecution is making different statements, saying "Seselj's volunteers," whereas the witness himself is talking about Seselj's men, and when the witness is saying "Seselj's men," it's because he heard this through hearsay, then the Prosecution is also adding the fact that Aleksic was reporting to Mr. Seselj. Therefore, when reading the summary, anyone would infer directly that Seselj's volunteers were on the ground in the area and that their boss, Aleksic, only reported to Mr. Seselj. Intellectually, this is how you construe this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe I was not very clear. We reported exactly what the witness said in the paragraph 13 of his statement, where he say -- 14, I'm sorry: "Aleksic was his own boss, probably reporting to Vojislav Seselj himself." It's what the witness said in paragraph 14 of his statement. Regarding this issue of Seselj volunteers, in paragraph 9 of the same statement, the witness says exactly: "Our task at the hill above the Jewish cemetery was to build the bunkers for the Seseljevci volunteers." So he refers to Seseljevci or volunteers in the same way, so it's not -- in the same sentence, he says "Seseljevci volunteers," so it means volunteers of Seselj's men. So I don't see any indiscrepancy [sic] or inconsistency among the statement and the summary that we draft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, the difference is great, and I understood it that you understood just how great the difference is. But the Prosecutor is trying to mask over something here, so "Seselj's volunteers" is one thing, volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, that is, which the party from Serbia sent in organised fashion as volunteers to the fronts, and it's also another matter altogether when a group of locals forms a unit and then they declare themselves as being Seseljevci or Seselj's men, whereas we're talking about locals from the area of Grbavica and other parts of Sarajevo, because the Serbian Radical Party never sent volunteers in organised fashion to the Jewish cemetery, and the Prosecutor does not have a single shred of evidence that it did do that. And may I continue now with my cross-examination, with your permission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-1060, you mentioned here the war events at Grbavica, and then you said that on several occasions, you saw how goods from certain flats were being loaded up into trucks with license plates from Serbia; Belgrade, Novi Sad and other places. Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, do you know that before the war, at Grbavica 1 and Grbavica 2, there were large numbers of active-duty and retired officers and non-commissioned officers of the JNA, that they lived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the larger garrisons was in Sarajevo, so quite possibly such people did exist. But I'd like to warn you or draw your attention to the following: They were not officers, taking away their own property. It was soldiers of the Serbian Republic doing that, loading up other people's property from other people's flats who had been expelled or where the tenants had fled, themselves. So my question to you is this: I never said and never knew, and I hear this for the first time now, that they were volunteers, Seselj's men or Chetniks. I never said that. I didn't know that they were volunteers. I knew that Chetniks existed or Seselj's men existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now I'm asking you this question not because I doubt that there was a lot of looting going on. I know that there was looting going on, and there was looting in all other areas as well. So I'm not challenging that fact, I'm not challenging that many flats were looted, if their owners had left and went elsewhere or left Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's not what I'm challenging. But in order to assess the magnitude of the looting that went on, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that there was a large exodus of the population, of active-duty officers and non-commissioned officers, JNA officers living in Grbavica, who were moving to Serbia because they were from Serbia originally, and that the army organised trucks to carry their goods to Serbia. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have that information. I do know that there were officers who lived on the territory of Grbavica, but I have to tell you that there was looting of homes and flats by people who'd been expelled and that they were being looted by the soldiers of the Serbian Republic, and that's what I claim, and you claim that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I know that there was looting, and that's not what I'm challenging. You said that individuals engaged in the looting and that the municipality issued certificates to them. Do you exclude the possibility, for instance, that there was a corrupt official in the municipality who, for some little money, would issue these certificates so that people who had looted other people's property received certificates saying that they were taking their own property out of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have that information, but I do have information that people came in who had looted other people's property and received certificates for that property. Now, whether they were compromised, or corrupt, or whether -- how they came by those certificates, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you do allow for the possibility that during the war, there was corruption when salaries were negligible and when life was difficult, clerks would write out certificates in return for a sum of money? That is possible; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't know that that was the case, but I'm just trying to look into all the possibilities. Right, you say "yes." Now, do you know that two check-points of the military police existed as you went towards Trebevic from Grbavica; do you know that to be a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see them. I went to Trebevic, but I never saw any ramps or check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At Raca, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't see a check-point there, a ramp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: My information tells me that those check-points were there. Now, when you were engaged in the work platoon, you said that you did not receive a salary or were not remunerated for your work in any way. I'm asking you, it's a serious question, because I have documents from Vogosca that those who worked in work platoon did receive a salary which was 20 per cent lower than a soldier's salary. Now, for the very first time, I'm hearing from you that civilians working at Grbavica working in a work platoon did not receive a salary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No civilian working in the work platoon received any remuneration, not one single dinar from the Serbian Republic, and I state that and I can bring in a lot of witnesses to testify to that effect, because a French soldier asked me, for example, when I was unloading humanitarian aid, he asked me, "How much do they pay you?" And I just laughed and said nothing, and he laughed too because he actually knew that we weren't remunerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the lunch that you were given while at work, as you said, did you receive any food stuffs that you could take home, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That never happened, nor did we have the right to anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How come, then -- how did the civilian population manage to survive for those three or actually four years of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Humanitarian aid arrived, and they received something from that or we went to market and bought those -- that humanitarian aid which the soldiers received and sold it at market.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At Grbavica 2, I lived by the shopping centre on Darijankovic Street, and I happened to be there in 1993 and 1994, and I saw with my own eyes when loaves of bread were brought in by the army for the whole settlement. Civilians gathered and formed lines, women mostly, and all received loaves of bread on the basis of a list. There were quite a lot of Muslims and I recognised them. They were my neighbours and I talked to them. Do you say that that is not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see or hear about it, and in Grbavica, please believe me when I say there was nothing like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was there any bread during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was flour, and we baked bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you mean to say there was no bread at Grbavica at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I saw this with my very own eyes in Grbavica. But, anyway, very well, Witness 1060. You mentioned a man here who was a terror to the work platoon, Aleksandar Trivkovic. Now, I did my best to find out who the man was, but nobody seems to have heard of him. Perhaps you mixed up some names there. Did you get the name wrong? This man, Aleksandar Trivkovic, nobody's heard of him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Many people didn't know what his name was, but they knew the nickname "Sasa," and everybody would know the name "Sasa," everybody working at the Zeljeznicar Football Club Stadium. Everybody would know the name "Sasa." I'm quite sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that Zoran Petkovic was the commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Nobody's ever heard of this man, Zoran Petkovic or Petrovic, but there was Aleksandar Petrovic, for example, and he, as a reserve officer, was the commander of the 2nd Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. So is it possible that you meant him instead of Zoran Petrovic, that it was Aleksandar Petrovic, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to correct you. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) and that you signed the document. This might be a public document. If that is the case, you might be identified. I'll ask the Registrar to hand down an order for redaction from line 3 onwards until line 9 of page 90. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I agree that this be redacted, but I was sent to see Zoran Petrovic. I was supposed to be protected. I was supposed to be under the protection of the United Nations. I went to speak to him, as the commander, and he said to me, "This is a state of war. Sir, go and do what you are ordered to do." So I had the right to go and ask for protection, but I didn't dare ask for it. What the gentleman here, the accused, is saying might be a mistake, but I was told to go to see this man, and I was in his office. He simply said to me, "There's a war on." I was over 65, so they should not have recruited me. It might be a mistake. His name might be something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear what the official title was of the unit commanded by Slavko Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You never heard that this was the Anti-Armour Company of the 2nd Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have a chance to talk to anyone about the names of these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. From these documents, I gave a translation in December. Please turn to page 498 and prepare page 499. We'll only look at these two pages today. It's also been translated into English. These are some pages from the military booklet of Slavko Aleksic. Mr. VS-1060, did you know that Slavko Aleksic was a captain of the Army of Republika Srpska, that that was his official rank, apart from the fact that I proclaimed him to be a Chetnik vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be shown for your sake and the sake of the Chamber? This is an order dated the 24th of September, 1993. Have you found it, pages 498 and 499?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that a military booklet or have I introduced some confusion into the proceedings? 498, you haven't found 498? It's 472 and 473. Those are different numbers here now. Do we have that now? First we see here that his rank is that of captain, pursuant to order number such-and-such, of a commander of the Army of Republika Srpska, and that's General Mladic, and we see the military post number on the stamp, 7512. Do you see the military post number? That's Lukavica? That was the military post to which Slavko Aleksic belonged. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm not putting this forward here because it's interesting for you. It's interesting for me and the Chamber. But you don't have any evidence to deny this or to challenge this, do you? I'm telling you here that he was a captain of the Army of Republika Srpska, promoted by order such-and-such, and you do not challenge this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I've heard this for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. Let's turn to the next page. Here we see Slavko Aleksic's participation in the war. He was in military post 1536/4, Han Pijesak, and the date is the 4th of April, 1992, to the 31st of May, 1993. That's his military post, the Command at Han Pijesak. You know about that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And here we have another military post, as of the 1st of June, 1993, up to the 31st of March 1996. That's military post 1512/7. I'm don't know whether I saw the first number correctly, but it might be a 7, 7512/7 Lukavica." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but I don't know why -- what this is for.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it confirms your statement that Slavko Aleksic was all the time an officer of the Army of Republika Srpska. There's nothing to challenge that, is there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, how could I know about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you said he was part of the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I assumed he was part of the Serbian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, now I'm confirming your supposition. May we continue this conversation without tension? I'm not showing you anything dangerous. I'm showing you this because it's in my interests to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have a document before us, like you have, which testifies to the fact that Aleksic is, from the 4th of April, 1992, onwards until the 31st of May, 1993, belongs to the military unit 1536-4. So if this document is a true document, nothing entitles us to claim that it is not the case, if this is a true document, this Slavko Aleksic was at the time a military -- he was entirely a military man. In your statement, in paragraph 11, you say that the vojvoda, that's Aleksic, was heading Seselj's men in Grbavica, and you even add after that that he had a black uniform. I don't know whether, in this unit 1536-4, what kind of uniform they were wearing, but I'm a little bit upset about what you are saying and what the document states, and I wonder about this. When you made your written statement, did you tell this to the investigator or is it the investigator who drafted this paragraph on the basis of the various information you gave him? Witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw Slavko Aleksic wearing a black uniform and a subara hat. This is the first time I have heard that he was a soldier and that he was promoted to the rank of captain. How and where this happened, I don't know. All I can say is that he commanded the Chetniks at the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You are telling us what you know, and I don't hold it against you that there are things you don't know. This is quite natural. You weren't involved in everything. You know only what you experienced yourself. I have a statement here signed by Slavko Aleksic, and he had his signature notarised in Bileca Municipality in Republika Srpska. Could we look at this statement marked with a Roman number I. I wish to go through it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ferrara, you are going to say that you don't have the translation, I assume, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. FERRARA
utterances.text: Yes, but I have my case manager who can translate it. But we received the statement only during the second break. Mr. Seselj received the statement at 1.00 this afternoon, so I think they could give us before starting the hearing today, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Mr. Seselj must have given the documents to the Registry at the beginning of the hearing, because when we arrived, we were given these documents. I believe that he must have given them as soon as he had them, since when we arrived at a quarter past 2.00, we had these documents on our table. Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I don't know why it says here at 1.04. I really did not receive it at 1.04 p.m. I received it at 2.00 p.m. I received 28 pages of documents, and I selected only two statements to use, and in the meantime I had to read them. I can't use something here without having read what it says beforehand. Maybe the Prosecutor can do that, but I can't. So this is a statement made by Slavko Aleksic, where he describes his war path, and I would like to go through the text and see whether you have any comments to make or something to say about it. He says that the beginning of the civil war found him in Sarajevo in Gornji Kovacici. Do you know where that neighbourhood is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's between Grbavica 1 and Skenderija near the hill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, underneath Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, where he was a sub-tenant at Trebevicka 73, which belonged to the Novo Sarajevo municipality, which numbered 120.000 inhabitants, of whom 60 per cent were of Serb ethnicity. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know in Sarajevo overall what the ethnic breakup was before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the entire canton --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, let's stick to the Sarajevo municipalities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were 158.000 Serbs living in Sarajevo. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the entire city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In full municipality or the suburbs as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the suburbs as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the highest concentration of Muslims was in Centar and Stari Grad municipalities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the highest concentration of Serbs was in the Novo Sarajevo municipality, leaving aside the municipalities in the suburbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So this could be correct, but neither you nor I have the entire data. So he says he arrived in Sarajevo in 1975 to study law and that he worked as a clerk in the main post office as of 1980. In early 1992, he says: "I and my neighbours, on our own initiative, organised ourselves because at night armed members of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets patrol the streets of our neighbourhood, by night. They would come there from other parts of Sarajevo, inhabited mostly by Muslims." Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't have this information. I was not organised in this way at all, nor did anyone tell me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, did you know that Grbavica 2, for example, at the beginning of the war, changed hands two or three times between the Serb and Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know anything of what happened in Grbavica 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. He goes on to say: "During the war, I was the commander of the Novo Sarajevo Chetnik Detachment, initially composed exclusively of local people, local men." He says -- well, now I'm interpreting what he says, that this detachment called itself "The new Sarajevo Chetnik Detachment." This was before the army of Republika Srpska was established; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. He goes on to say in late 1992 and early 1993, volunteers started arriving, first Russians, then Bulgarians, Macedonians, Greeks, Serbs from America, and even a man from Japan. Did you hear that there were Russians in his unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw them myself. I saw the Greeks, too, and the Belorussian, because I spoke Russian, so I could communicate with them; and I know that they arrived there. But I didn't know about the Japanese.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you know about the Bulgarians, Macedonians and Greeks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that various people came, but I didn't know how many there were and I wasn't really interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. He goes on to say there were very few volunteers from Serbia and they were isolated cases: "I assert with full liability that there was no organised arrival of volunteers organised by the Serbian Radical Party." Did you hear that the Serbian Radical Party sent volunteers to this unit in an organised manner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. Please allow me to interrupt you. If what Mr. Aleksic is saying is true, well, you had said that also, as a matter of fact, when you answered Mr. Ferrara's questions. It seems that in Mr. Aleksic's unit, there were Bulgarians, Russians, Macedonians, and so on and so forth. I think there was even a Japanese person. So how is it that -- and you seem to confirm this, since as you spoke Russian, you spoke Russian with Russians and Belorussian, so you knew that in this new unit, there were people who came from other countries, who did not come from Serbia, so how is it that you, before the OTP investigators, you said that these were Seselj's men, whereas a Russian -- what would enable you to infer that a Russian, or Bulgarian, or Japanese is one of Seselj's men? So why did you refer to Seselj's men when you talked about Slavko Aleksic's unit, when we have information that would lead us to believe that this unit comprised a number of foreigners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that I didn't know to whom these foreigners belonged, but I did see them at Grbavica, and I talked to them too. I know that cars that were, well, Volvos and Lada-type cars that were out of order, they took spare parts from those cars. Now, which unit they belonged to, I don't know. I didn't know whether they belonged to any of the units of the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You should know which parties were active in Sarajevo before the war. There was the Serbian Democratic Party, the Party of Democratic Action, the Croatian Democratic Union, and some others; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Those were the parties that incorporated the Serbs, the Muslims, the Croats. Then there was the former Communist Party and some others. Did you ever hear of the existence of the Serbian Radical Party in Sarajevo before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that during the war, its board was established for the Novo Sarajevo municipality, precisely at Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If I tell you at sometime toward the end of 1992, Slavko Aleksic transferred from the Serbian Democratic Party to the Serbian Radical Party and formed a board of the Serbian Radical Party at Grbavica for the whole of the Novo Sarajevo municipality, do you believe me if I tell you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't claim either way, I can't say I believe you or don't believe you, because I wasn't involved in any of that. I didn't know what was going on in the parties at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. But you didn't hear of the existence of the Serbian Radical Party before the war at all, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's see what Slavko Aleksic says in continuation, in addition to the fact that he says that there was no organised arrival of the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party to his unit. He goes on to say the following: "The detachment fought within the composition of the Army of Republika Srpska and it was in the composition of the 3rd Infantry Battalion under the command of Major Blagoje Kovacevic, under the name of the Anti-Armoured Company or the 5th Company, and the 3rd Infantry Battalion belonged to the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade under the command of Colonel Veljko Stojanovic. So he identifies the commander of this brigade as being Colonel Veljko Stojanovic, and you gave us another name. So could it be that this was just be an an error on your part, or what do you say to that? Leave it on our screens, please, the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the first time that I hear of this name and surname like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Slavko Aleksic goes on to say the chief of staff was Lieutenant-Colonel Pero Sajlovic [phoen]: "By virtue of the order from the command of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, I was given the rank of captain and demobilised as captain on the 31st of March, 1996." Now, do you know that Slavko Aleksic was not an active officer before the war? We've already seen that, haven't we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was an ordinary soldier, private, and he reached the rank of captain based on his war merits; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that would roughly be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, Slavko Aleksic goes on to say, Grbavica was defended by just one army, the Army of Republika Srpska, with its united command. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, one can assume that that was the case, and I think that's what I said too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now turn to page 2, please. It says: "As there were no uniforms, the soldiers were dressed in different ways. Usually, they were wearing civilian clothes or combined with certain parts of a military uniform." And this corresponds to what you said, that people were dressed differently at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, the officers, he says, paid great care and attention that no parts of the uniform should be black or entirely black, because we knew that this could cause negative emotions among the non-Serb population that lived in Grbavica. And for a long time throughout 1992, in fact, there were no insignia of the cockade type because we couldn't come by them anywhere. And this brings us to a collision between what you say and what Aleksic says, because he claims that black uniforms quite simply did not exist, nor were they permitted, whereas you say you saw him wearing a black uniform. Perhaps you were misled by a black -- his black beard. That's a black beard, sir. You showed us Slavko Aleksic's photograph, just showing his face and a black beard, and the Prosecution has Slavko Aleksic's photograph showing him always wearing a camouflage uniform, but the Prosecution is hiding those photographs now because it suits the Prosecution for you to think that he was wearing a black uniform. You saw Slavko Aleksic earlier on, Judges, wearing a camouflage uniform, and I can't keep collecting all those photographs. I find it difficult to find my way in all the material and documents, anyway. But, anyway, that's not an essential point, and discrepancies like that are normal. I don't hold it against you, I really don't hold anything against you, because I think you testified to the best of your memory, and I respect that. But we'll go through these different things because various people remember various things, different things. You're an intellectual, so every man has his own vision of things; right? Now, the company that I was in command goes on to say: "Defended positions from the top of the Jewish cemetery." That's the old Jewish cemetery, isn't is it, that hasn't been in use for a long time. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Nobody's been buried there for decades. It dates back to who knows what times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the arrival of the Jews in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the whole area is known under the name of Jewish cemetery. Up until [indiscernible] 1 to feature 942, Debelo Brdo, where it touched upon the 2nd Company of the 3rd Infantry Battalion so that we never had any control over the Beogradska, Ljubljanska, Radnicka, or any other street, settlement, or part of a settlement. That's what he says. That these streets, the ones you mentioned, they did not control. They had a line right from the Jewish cemetery, the top of the Jewish cemetery, up to feature 945 and Debelo Brdo. Do you know where Debelo Brdo was, where the observation post of the United Nations was later on; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So that's the area held by his unit, that's what he says, and he says that in the streets mentioned here, they had nothing to do with them. They could go down there, but they were not in control of that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to put you right, because behind their backs here, behind the backs -- well, they passed by those streets to reach the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. So we agree on that point. Now, all responsibility for the safety and security of civilians within the settlement was borne by the civilian police, he says, whose police station was located in General Draza Mihajlovic Street. Do you know what name was renamed -- what street was renamed into General Draza Mihajlovic Street later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zagrebacka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's the longest street in Grbavica. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that there was a police station there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That police station was in charge of providing security and safety for the citizens; right? Now, how it did that is another matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would have been better had that police not existed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's move on. That's not the subject of our discussion here. Slavko Aleksic goes on to say the distance from the enemy positions was measured by the width of a street or the length of a house, so that it was physically impossible for somebody to find themselves in a crossfire on what was called no man's land, because the enemy, by precise targets, would thwart any attempt to emerge from a shelter. Is it true that the lines that he held were very close to the Muslim lines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How would I know that? How do I know what the distance between the two frontlines was? I couldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you worked in the area of the Jewish cemetery and you had to defend yourself from the fire from your own compatriots who didn't know who they were shooting at or who was doing the shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just worked on a hill above the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. He goes on did say Grbavica was under continuous enemy sniper fire and many civilians were killed, about 904 or 940, I'm not quite sure, mostly Serbs. The number of civilians from other ethnic groups that were killed by the sniper fire was proportionate to their representation in the population of Grbavica, that is to say, far less. So do you know of the people killed by sniper fire on the Muslim side, these large figures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't keep records. I couldn't know about that. I was in the work platoon. Now, when they were killed, whether that was during the day or during the night, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. But there is information telling us that over 900 people were killed by sniper fire and that these were mostly Serbs, although Muslims and others were killed too. I know for a fact that a lot of children were killed by sniper fire. Did you ever hear of a child being killed by sniper fire on Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't have that information or records. There were just rumours. How would I know about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Well, he says -- Slavko Aleksic also says that the name Aleksandar Trivkovic, Sasa, is quite unknown to him, and he stresses that there was never a soldier under his command by that name. So do you agree that even if he does exist, he wasn't under Slavko Aleksic's unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't claim that he belonged to Aleksic, but that he was a soldier of the Serbian Republic and that he was up at the positions around the football pitch, the Zeljeznicar Football Club's pitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, he goes on to speak about the use of the work platoons: "My unit determined the defence line, and this was done by 90 per cent of the soldiers whom I commanded, and the work platoon together with the soldiers, they provided the defence." Now, as far as I know, on the basis of the laws -- is it true that the civilian authorities organised the work platoons and managed them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This man, Dilmar whom I mentioned, was a soldier, so he decided who was going to work where.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As an intellectual, you must know there was a law governing the total national defence before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So do you know that he was in charge -- that that law prescribed for all types of rights and duties, military and work obligations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Slavko Aleksic says he never went into a cafe named "Chetnik," and that no such cafe existed in Grbavica, but that the following cafes existed; Kokarda, Krune, Apollo and Neretva. Is that a mistake? Perhaps you thought that Kokarda or Cockade Cafe was called the Chetnik Cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in Radnicka Street. I don't know the number but there was a cafe that was Chetnik. I didn't claim that Aleksic went there. All I said was I saw him passing by, but I didn't claim that he was in the cafe itself, that there were Chetniks there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This is what he says: "The fighters of the 5th Anti-Armoured Fighting Company were prohibited alcoholic drinks, and even in special -- on special occasions. Sanctioning alcoholism was very strict in the VRS, and particular attention was made to that on Grbavica because the multi-ethnicity of the population, because they are exposed to enemy fire all the time." Turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note this is much too fast for interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is not a single army in the world --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The interpreters ask you to slow down because you're reading out too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wanted to get through the document by 7.00, but it doesn't appear that I'm going to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you see soldiers from Slavko Aleksic's units drunk ever or see him drunk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that he was sitting and drinking anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear that I came to Grbavica during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was rumoured, but I never saw you. I didn't see you come, nor did I know whether you were there, but people said that you were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I was at Grbavica 1. I went up to the frontline at Ljubljana Most, and I was at the marketplace in Grbavica 1 and 2. And whenever I went to visit Slavko Aleksic's unit, there was only fruit juice served there, ordinary water, nothing more than that, that there was not a single drop of alcoholic beverage in that unit ever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How could I know that? How do you expect me to know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, do you have reason to doubt it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that I'm an anti-alcoholic, just like Slavko Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know. I've never had an opportunity of discussing your behaviour or your habits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now he goes on to say that in his unit, there were volunteers from different countries. He repeats that, and he says that there were no men sent by the Serbian Radical Party, but does say there were soldiers who had different affiliations, members of the Serbian Radical Party, that is to say locals, the Serbian Democratic Party, the Serbian National Renewal, but all those soldiers were from Sarajevo, he says. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have that information, nor could I have it, nor did I need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at these last two paragraphs, if we manage to do so in the three minutes we have left: "As soon as the unit was formed, I read out the Geneva Conventions to all the soldiers and drew their attention to the fact that they must be particularly careful in their conduct towards Muslim civilians and Croats, so I say with full responsibility that not I, nor any soldiers under my command, ever inflicted any injustice to Muslim or Croat, let alone a single crime throughout the war being committed." He says that and refers to his own unit. So we don't exclude the fact that there were crimes committed, but he guarantees that nobody from his particular unit committed any crime whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have any of these cases, what the conduct and behaviour was of individual units. That wasn't something that I could know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. He goes on to say, with respect to all these names, he says: "I'm sure that in Grbavica there was not a single officer named Zoran Petkovic. I knew Aleksandar Petrovic, and I was on friendly terms with him. Aleksandar Petrovic was a reserve captain by rank, the commander of the 2nd Infantry Battalion. However, he was never a superior officer to me. Establishment-wise, we had no points in common. He was the command of the 2nd Battalion, and my company belonged to the 3rd Battalion, so that I was under the direct command of the commander of the battalion, that is to say major Blagoje Kovacevic. He was establishment-wise under the command of the Command of the brigade, that is to say, Colonel Veljko Stojanovic." So that is the cadre structure and hierarchical chain of command that Slavko Aleksic was in. Do you believe him when he says all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the possibility of establishing whether he's telling the truth or not. I made my statement. I said that there were Russians, Ukrainians, Belorussians, Greeks, even Bulgarians. We all knew that. Now, who these men belonged to, I really didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope I have more time tomorrow, Judges, a bit more time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have a bit more time left for tomorrow. I believe that you have 27 or 28 minutes left. Witness, unfortunately your hearing couldn't be completely finished today. We will have to resume tomorrow, so at 2.15 p.m., because we're sitting in the afternoon. You made the solemn declaration earlier, so you are now in the hands of justice. You're not supposed to have any contact with Mr. Ferrara, and I wanted to remind you of this. I will now adjourn the hearing, and wish everyone a good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 25th day of June, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
